notes.front: What is Azure Virtual Machines?
notes.back: A service for deploying and managing virtual machines inside an Azure virtual network.
notes.explanation: It is the infrastructure-as-a-service option: Microsoft manages the infrastructure and you manage the machines.
notes.example: Like renting a server in someone else's data centre, except you create it in minutes and choose its size from a menu.
notes.source: Choose an Azure compute service (MicrosoftDocs architecture-center), “Understand the basic features”
notes.evidence: Azure Virtual Machines is a service that you can use to deploy and manage virtual machines (VMs) inside an Azure virtual network.

notes.front: What are Azure Spot Virtual Machines?
notes.back: Virtual machines that run on Azure's unused capacity at a significant discount, and are evicted when Azure needs the capacity back.
notes.explanation: The discount comes from using spare capacity, which Azure can reclaim at any time.
notes.example: Like a standby airline seat: much cheaper, but you may be bumped off when a full-fare passenger turns up.
notes.source: Azure Spot Virtual Machines (MicrosoftDocs azure-compute-docs), “Azure Spot Virtual Machines”
notes.evidence: Using Azure Spot Virtual Machines allows you to take advantage of our unused capacity at a significant cost savings. At any point in time when Azure needs the capacity back, the Azure infrastructure will evict Azure Spot Virtual Machines.

notes.front: What is Azure Dedicated Host?
notes.back: A service that provides physical servers, assigned to one Azure subscription, that host one or more of your virtual machines.
notes.explanation: The servers are the same ones used in Azure data centres, offered as a directly accessible hardware resource.
notes.example: Like renting a whole house instead of a flat in a shared block: nobody else lives in the building.
notes.source: Azure Dedicated Hosts (MicrosoftDocs azure-compute-docs), “Azure Dedicated Hosts”
notes.evidence: Azure Dedicated Host is a service that provides physical servers able to host one or more virtual machines assigned to one Azure subscription. Dedicated hosts are the same physical servers used in our data centers, provided instead as a directly accessible hardware resource.

notes.front: What is a proximity placement group?
notes.back: A logical grouping that makes sure Azure compute resources are physically located close to each other.
notes.explanation: It is useful for workloads where low latency between machines is a requirement.
notes.example: Like asking a hotel to put the whole team on the same corridor so meetings start without a long walk.
notes.source: Proximity placement groups (MicrosoftDocs azure-compute-docs), “Proximity placement groups”
notes.evidence: A proximity placement group is a logical grouping used to make sure that Azure compute resources are physically located close to each other. Proximity placement groups are useful for workloads where low latency is a requirement.

notes.front: In Azure managed disks, what does SSD stand for?
notes.back: Solid-state drive, as in the Premium SSD v2, Premium SSD and Standard SSD disk types.
notes.explanation: Three of the five managed disk type names use it.
notes.example: Like the flash storage in a modern laptop, rather than a spinning platter.
notes.source: Azure managed disk types (MicrosoftDocs azure-compute-docs), “Azure managed disk types”
notes.evidence: Ultra Disk - Premium SSD v2 - Premium SSD (solid-state drive) - Standard SSD - Standard HDD (hard disk drive)

notes.front: In Azure managed disks, what does HDD stand for?
notes.back: Hard disk drive: the drive type behind the Standard HDD disk type.
notes.explanation: Standard HDD is the one managed disk type named for it.
notes.example: Like the spinning disk in an older desktop computer: cheaper per gigabyte, but slower than flash.
notes.source: Azure managed disk types (MicrosoftDocs azure-compute-docs), “Azure managed disk types”
notes.evidence: Ultra Disk - Premium SSD v2 - Premium SSD (solid-state drive) - Standard SSD - Standard HDD (hard disk drive)

notes.front: What are Azure Ultra Disks?
notes.back: The highest-performing storage option for Azure virtual machines.
notes.explanation: They suit data-intensive workloads such as top-tier databases and transaction-heavy workloads.
notes.example: Like fitting a racing engine to a car: the fastest disk on offer, priced for the jobs that need it.
notes.source: Azure managed disk types (MicrosoftDocs azure-compute-docs), “Ultra Disks”
notes.evidence: Azure Ultra Disks are the highest-performing storage option for Azure virtual machines (VMs). You can change the performance parameters of an Ultra Disk without having to restart your VMs. Ultra Disks are suited for data-intensive workloads such as SAP HANA, top-tier databases, and transaction-heavy workloads.

notes.front: What is Azure VMware Solution (AVS)?
notes.back: A service providing private clouds that contain VMware vSphere clusters built from dedicated bare-metal Azure infrastructure.
notes.explanation: It is available in Azure Commercial and Azure Government.
notes.example: Like moving your on-premises VMware estate into an Azure data centre and keeping the same tools to run it.
notes.source: What is Azure VMware Solution? (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “What is Azure VMware Solution?”
notes.evidence: Azure VMware Solution provides private clouds that contain VMware vSphere clusters built from dedicated bare-metal Azure infrastructure. Azure VMware Solution is available in Azure Commercial and Azure Government.

notes.front: What is Azure App Service?
notes.back: A platform for running web applications, mobile back ends and RESTful APIs without managing the underlying infrastructure.
notes.explanation: You don't manage the underlying infrastructure yourself.
notes.example: Like handing your website's code to a hosting company that runs, patches and scales the servers for you.
notes.source: App Service overview (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “App Service overview”
notes.evidence: Azure App Service is a platform that lets you run web applications, mobile back ends, and RESTful APIs without worrying about managing the underlying infrastructure.

notes.front: What is an App Service plan?
notes.back: The set of compute resources that App Service apps run on; every App Service app runs in one.
notes.explanation: Azure Functions can also use App Service plans in some scenarios.
notes.example: Like a server farm you rent for your web apps: every app you add shares the same rented machines.
notes.source: What are Azure App Service plans? (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “What are Azure App Service plans?”
notes.evidence: An *Azure App Service plan* defines a set of compute resources for a web app to run. An app service always runs in an App Service plan. Azure Functions also use App Service plans in some scenarios.

notes.front: What is Azure Container Instances (ACI)?
notes.back: The fastest and simplest way to run Linux or Windows containers in Azure, without managing virtual machines or adopting a higher-level service.
notes.explanation: Microsoft notes that containers are becoming the preferred way to package, deploy and manage cloud applications.
notes.example: Like hailing a taxi for one trip instead of buying and maintaining a fleet of cars.
notes.source: What is Azure Container Instances? (MicrosoftDocs azure-compute-docs), “What is Azure Container Instances?”
notes.evidence: Containers are becoming the preferred way to package, deploy, and manage cloud applications. Azure Container Instances offers the fastest and simplest way to run Linux or Windows containers in Azure, without having to manage any virtual machines and without having to adopt a higher-level service.

notes.front: In Azure Container Instances, what is a container group?
notes.back: Several containers scheduled together that share the same host, local network, storage and lifecycle.
notes.explanation: It lets a main application container run alongside supporting containers such as logging sidecars.
notes.example: Like a band that always travels in one van: they arrive together, share the gear and leave together.
notes.source: What is Azure Container Instances? (MicrosoftDocs azure-compute-docs), “Run multiple containers in a single container group”
notes.evidence: Azure Container Instances supports scheduling of multiple containers within a single container group that share the same container host, local network, storage, and lifecycle. This enables you to combine your main application container with other supporting role containers, such as logging sidecars.

notes.front: What is Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)?
notes.back: A managed Kubernetes service for deploying and managing containerised applications.
notes.explanation: It shifts the complexity and operational overhead of managing Kubernetes to Azure.
notes.example: Like running your own Kubernetes cluster, but Azure builds and looks after the control plane for you.
notes.source: What is Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)? (MicrosoftDocs azure-aks-docs), “What is Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)?”
notes.evidence: Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) is a managed Kubernetes service for deploying and managing containerized applications. AKS offloads the complexity and operational overhead of managing Kubernetes to Azure.

notes.front: What is Azure Container Apps?
notes.back: A serverless platform for running containerised applications without managing the underlying infrastructure.
notes.explanation: It takes on server configuration, container orchestration and deployment details, which reduces operational overhead.
notes.example: Like Kubernetes with the cluster hidden: you hand over containers and scaling rules, and the platform does the rest.
notes.source: Azure Container Apps overview (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Azure Container Apps overview”
notes.evidence: Azure Container Apps is a serverless platform for running containerized applications without managing the underlying infrastructure. Instead of configuring servers, orchestrating containers, and handling deployment details yourself, let Container Apps provide the up-to-date resources that keep your applications stable, secure, and scalable. This approach reduces operational overhead

notes.front: What is Azure Functions?
notes.back: A serverless solution for building apps with less code and infrastructure, where the cloud provides the resources to keep them running.
notes.explanation: You focus on your code, and Functions handles deploying and maintaining servers.
notes.example: Like a light that switches on by motion sensor: code runs only when something triggers it.
notes.source: What is Azure Functions? (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “What is Azure Functions?”
notes.evidence: Azure Functions is a serverless solution that allows you to build robust apps while using less code, and with less infrastructure and lower costs. Instead of worrying about deploying and maintaining servers, you can use the cloud infrastructure to provide all the up-to-date resources needed to keep your applications running.

notes.front: What is the Flex Consumption plan for Azure Functions?
notes.back: The recommended Functions hosting plan, with fast event-driven scaling, virtual network integration and pay-as-you-go billing.
notes.explanation: It is the serverless plan Microsoft points new function apps to.
notes.example: Like a taxi meter for code: you pay for the trips taken, and more taxis join the rank as the queue grows.
notes.source: What is Azure Functions? (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Hosting options”
notes.evidence: | Flex Consumption plan | **Recommended.** Fast event-driven scaling, virtual network integration, and pay-as-you-go billing. |

notes.front: What is Azure Logic Apps?
notes.back: A cloud service for automating business process workflows and integrating services, systems, apps and data, with little or no code.
notes.explanation: It works across cloud, on-premises and hybrid environments.
notes.example: Like drawing a flowchart of 'when an order arrives, check the amount, then email a manager', and having it run for real.
notes.source: What is Azure Logic Apps? (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “What is Azure Logic Apps?”
notes.evidence: Azure Logic Apps is a cloud service and platform for automating enterprise business process workflows and integrating services, systems, apps, and data across cloud, on-premises, and hybrid environments with little or no code.

notes.front: What is Azure Batch?
notes.back: A service that runs large-scale parallel and high-performance computing batch jobs, managing a pool of compute nodes and scheduling jobs on them.
notes.explanation: There is no cluster or job scheduler software for you to install, manage or scale.
notes.example: Like hiring a render farm by the hour: you hand over the frames, and the farm spreads them across its machines.
notes.source: What is Azure Batch? (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “What is Azure Batch?”
notes.evidence: Azure Batch creates and manages a pool of compute nodes (virtual machines), installs the applications you want to run, and schedules jobs to run on the nodes. There's no cluster or job scheduler software to install, manage, or scale.

notes.front: Microsoft's compute decision flowchart starts by splitting into which two branches?
notes.back: Migrate an existing workload, or build a new one.
notes.explanation: The migrate branch asks whether the application is cloud-optimised and whether it can be lifted and shifted.
notes.source: Choose an Azure compute service (MicrosoftDocs architecture-center), “Architecture”
notes.evidence: The flowchart begins with a start node and splits into two primary branches labeled migrate and build new. The migrate branch includes decision points that assess whether the application is optimized for the cloud and whether it can be lifted and shifted.

notes.front: In the compute decision guide, what does lift and shift mean?
notes.back: Migrating a workload to the cloud without redesigning the application or changing code; also called rehosting.
notes.explanation: Microsoft recommends a like-for-like migration first, deferring optimisation unless time and budget allow redesign.
notes.source: Choose an Azure compute service (MicrosoftDocs architecture-center), “Architecture”
notes.evidence: A strategy for migrating a workload to the cloud without redesigning the application or making code changes. It's also known as *rehosting*. We recommend that workload teams that perform migrations use a like-for-like approach and defer optimization unless their timeline and budget support redesign for cloud-native functionality.

notes.front: In the compute decision guide, what is the cloud-optimised strategy?
notes.back: Migrating by refactoring an application to use cloud-native features; it also describes new workloads designed that way.
notes.explanation: It also fits greenfield workloads designed for cloud-native features from the start.
notes.source: Choose an Azure compute service (MicrosoftDocs architecture-center), “Architecture”
notes.evidence: A strategy for migrating to the cloud by refactoring an application to take advantage of cloud-native features and capabilities. You can also use this strategy to describe greenfield (new) workloads designed from the start to use cloud-native features.

notes.front: A workload has several distinct compute components. How should you choose compute for it?
notes.back: Evaluate each component's needs separately; a complete solution can use two or more compute services.
notes.explanation: Different components can have different compute needs.
notes.source: Choose an Azure compute service (MicrosoftDocs architecture-center), “Architecture”
notes.evidence: If your workload consists of distinct compute components, evaluate each application's needs separately. A complete solution can include two or more compute services.

notes.front: Can any of the compute platforms in Microsoft's decision guide run across several regions by themselves?
notes.back: No. All of them are regional; a multiregion design needs external routing in front of an instance in each region.
notes.explanation: Active-active or active-passive designs across regions need external routing.
notes.source: Choose an Azure compute service (MicrosoftDocs architecture-center), “Built-in multiregion capabilities”
notes.evidence: All of the application platforms that this decision guide addresses are regional. They require external routing to enable multiregion topologies, such as active-active for resiliency or active-passive for recoverability.

notes.front: A DevOps team with deep Kubernetes expertise needs full control of cluster management and upgrades for containerised services. Which service fits their skills best?
notes.back: Azure Kubernetes Service.
notes.choices:
A) Azure Kubernetes Service
B) Azure Container Apps
C) Azure App Service
notes.choicesExplained: B: Container Apps abstracts Kubernetes management away, for teams that don't want its complexity. C: App Service suits developers focused on code, not cluster management.
notes.explanation: The guide lists AKS as best for DevOps teams that have Kubernetes expertise, with high operational overhead.
notes.source: Choose an Azure compute service (MicrosoftDocs architecture-center), “Team skills and operational overhead”
notes.evidence: | AKS | Kubernetes administration, container orchestration | High: Cluster management, upgrades, security | DevOps teams that have Kubernetes expertise |

notes.front: A small team of web developers wants to deploy code with low operational overhead and no infrastructure skills. Which service does the guide match to them?
notes.back: Azure App Service.
notes.choices:
A) Azure App Service
B) Azure Virtual Machines
C) Azure Kubernetes Service
notes.choicesExplained: B: virtual machines need operating system administration and patching, with high overhead. C: AKS needs Kubernetes administration skills.
notes.explanation: The guide pairs App Service with application developers focused on code, and low operational overhead.
notes.source: Choose an Azure compute service (MicrosoftDocs architecture-center), “Team skills and operational overhead”
notes.evidence: | App Service | Web development, application deployment | Low: Platform handles infrastructure | Application developers focused on code |

notes.front: Which hosting model lets you provision virtual machines with their networking and storage, and is most similar to a traditional on-premises environment?
notes.back: Infrastructure as a service (IaaS).
notes.explanation: Microsoft manages the infrastructure, and you manage the virtual machines.
notes.source: Choose an Azure compute service (MicrosoftDocs architecture-center), “Understand the hosting models”
notes.evidence: Infrastructure as a service (IaaS) lets you provision VMs along with the associated networking and storage components. You can then deploy any software and applications on those VMs. This model is the most similar to a traditional on-premises environment. Microsoft manages the infrastructure, and you manage the VMs.

notes.front: Which hosting model provides a managed environment where you deploy an application without managing virtual machines?
notes.back: Platform as a service (PaaS).
notes.explanation: App Service and Container Apps are the guide's examples of this model.
notes.source: Choose an Azure compute service (MicrosoftDocs architecture-center), “Understand the hosting models”
notes.evidence: Platform as a service (PaaS) provides a managed hosting environment where you can deploy your application without the need to manage VMs. App Service and Container Apps are PaaS services.

notes.front: Which hosting model lets you deploy code to a service that runs it automatically?
notes.back: Functions as a service (FaaS).
notes.explanation: Azure Functions is the guide's example of this model.
notes.source: Choose an Azure compute service (MicrosoftDocs architecture-center), “Understand the hosting models”
notes.evidence: Functions as a service (FaaS) lets you deploy your code to the service, which automatically runs it. Azure Functions is a FaaS service.

notes.front: Which hosting model does Azure Functions belong to?
notes.back: Functions as a service (FaaS).
notes.explanation: The guide names Azure Functions as its example of this model.
notes.source: Choose an Azure compute service (MicrosoftDocs architecture-center), “Understand the hosting models”
notes.evidence: Azure Functions is a FaaS service.

notes.front: IaaS versus FaaS: which gives the most control, and which manages nearly everything for you?
notes.back: IaaS gives the most control, flexibility and portability; FaaS manages nearly all aspects of running the application.
notes.explanation: The trade-off runs between control and ease of management, with PaaS in between.
notes.source: Choose an Azure compute service (MicrosoftDocs architecture-center), “Understand the hosting models”
notes.evidence: A trade-off exists between control and ease of management. IaaS provides the most control, flexibility, and portability, but you must provision, set up, and manage the VMs and network components that you create. FaaS services automatically manage nearly all aspects of running an application. PaaS provides partial management and requires some user configuration.

notes.front: Which virtual machine size type offers a balanced processor-to-memory ratio for testing, small databases and low-traffic web servers?
notes.back: General purpose.
notes.explanation: The balance suits development and test, small to medium databases and low to medium traffic web servers.
notes.source: Sizes for virtual machines in Azure (MicrosoftDocs azure-compute-docs), “General purpose”
notes.evidence: General purpose VM sizes provide balanced CPU-to-memory ratio. Ideal for testing and development, small to medium databases, and low to medium traffic web servers.

notes.front: Which virtual machine size type has a high processor-to-memory ratio, suiting network appliances, batch processes and application servers?
notes.back: Compute optimised.
notes.explanation: A high processor-to-memory ratio favours processing over memory.
notes.source: Sizes for virtual machines in Azure (MicrosoftDocs azure-compute-docs), “Compute optimized”
notes.evidence: Compute optimized VM sizes have a high CPU-to-memory ratio. These sizes are good for medium traffic web servers, network appliances, batch processes, and application servers.

notes.front: Which virtual machine size type has a high memory-to-processor ratio for relational database servers, caches and in-memory analytics?
notes.back: Memory optimised.
notes.explanation: Those workloads hold large amounts of data in memory.
notes.source: Sizes for virtual machines in Azure (MicrosoftDocs azure-compute-docs), “Memory optimized”
notes.evidence: Memory optimized VM sizes offer a high memory-to-CPU ratio that is great for relational database servers, medium to large caches, and in-memory analytics.

notes.front: Which virtual machine size type offers high disk throughput and input/output for big data, NoSQL databases and data warehousing?
notes.back: Storage optimised.
notes.explanation: Its examples include Cassandra, MongoDB and Redis.
notes.source: Sizes for virtual machines in Azure (MicrosoftDocs azure-compute-docs), “Storage optimized”
notes.evidence: Storage optimized virtual machine (VM) sizes offer high disk throughput and IO, and are ideal for Big Data, SQL, NoSQL databases, data warehousing, and large transactional databases. Examples include Cassandra, MongoDB, Cloudera, and Redis.

notes.front: Which virtual machine size type offers single, multiple or fractional graphics processors for graphics-intensive and visualisation work?
notes.back: Graphics processing unit accelerated.
notes.explanation: These specialised sizes target compute-intensive, graphics-intensive and visualisation workloads.
notes.source: Sizes for virtual machines in Azure (MicrosoftDocs azure-compute-docs), “GPU accelerated”
notes.evidence: GPU optimized VM sizes are specialized virtual machines available with single, multiple, or fractional GPUs. These sizes are designed for compute-intensive, graphics-intensive, and visualization workloads.

notes.front: Which virtual machine size type provides single or multiple field-programmable gate arrays for compute-intensive work?
notes.back: Field-programmable gate array accelerated.
notes.explanation: These specialised sizes are designed for compute-intensive workloads.
notes.source: Sizes for virtual machines in Azure (MicrosoftDocs azure-compute-docs), “FPGA accelerated”
notes.evidence: FPGA optimized VM sizes are specialized virtual machines available with single or multiple FPGAs. These sizes are designed for compute-intensive workloads.

notes.front: Which virtual machine size type is optimised for workloads such as fluid dynamics, weather simulation and financial risk analysis?
notes.back: High performance compute.
notes.explanation: These sizes target simulation and analysis workloads that need large-scale computation.
notes.source: Sizes for virtual machines in Azure (MicrosoftDocs azure-compute-docs), “High performance compute”
notes.evidence: Azure High Performance Compute VMs are optimized for various HPC workloads such as computational fluid dynamics, finite element analysis, frontend and backend EDA, rendering, molecular dynamics, computational geoscience, weather simulation, and financial risk analysis.

notes.front: A relational database server keeps a large working set in memory and needs far more memory than processor. Which size type fits?
notes.back: Memory optimised.
notes.choices:
A) Compute optimised
B) Memory optimised
C) General purpose
notes.choicesExplained: A: compute optimised has a high processor-to-memory ratio, the reverse of what is needed. C: general purpose is balanced and suits small to medium databases.
notes.explanation: Memory optimised sizes have a high memory-to-processor ratio suited to relational database servers.
notes.source: Sizes for virtual machines in Azure (MicrosoftDocs azure-compute-docs), “Memory optimized”
notes.evidence: Memory optimized VM sizes offer a high memory-to-CPU ratio that is great for relational database servers, medium to large caches, and in-memory analytics.

notes.front: What does each character in an Azure virtual machine size name represent?
notes.back: A different aspect of the machine, such as its family, number of virtual processors and extra features like premium storage.
notes.explanation: Reading the name tells you what the size offers.
notes.source: Sizes for virtual machines in Azure (MicrosoftDocs azure-compute-docs), “VM size and series naming”
notes.evidence: Azure VM sizes follow specific naming conventions to denote varying features and specifications. Each character in the name represents different aspects of the VM. These include the VM family, number of vCPUs, and extra features like premium storage or included accelerators.

notes.front: What availability promise comes with Azure Spot Virtual Machines, and how much notice precedes eviction?
notes.back: No service-level agreement or high availability guarantee; eviction comes with 30 seconds' notice.
notes.explanation: Azure takes the capacity back whenever it needs it.
notes.source: Azure Spot Virtual Machines (MicrosoftDocs azure-compute-docs), “Azure Spot Virtual Machines”
notes.evidence: Azure will allocate the VMs if there's capacity available, but there's no SLA for these VMs. An Azure Spot Virtual Machine offers no high availability guarantees. At any point in time when Azure needs the capacity back, the Azure infrastructure will evict Azure Spot Virtual Machines with 30-seconds notice.

notes.front: What are the two reasons a Spot virtual machine can be evicted?
notes.back: Azure needs the capacity for pay-as-you-go workloads, or the Spot price rises above the maximum price you set.
notes.explanation: You choose the maximum price yourself when you create the machine.
notes.source: Azure Spot Virtual Machines (MicrosoftDocs azure-compute-docs), “Eviction policy”
notes.evidence: Spot VMs can be stopped if Azure needs capacity for other pay-as-you-go workloads or when the price of the spot instance exceeds the maximum price that you have set.

notes.front: Spot eviction policies Deallocate versus Delete: which keeps charging you for disk storage?
notes.back: Deallocate (the default); it keeps the stopped machine and its disks. Delete removes the machine and its disks.
notes.explanation: Deallocated machines also count against quota, and redeploying them later isn't guaranteed.
notes.source: Azure Spot Virtual Machines (MicrosoftDocs azure-compute-docs), “Eviction policy”
notes.evidence: The *Deallocate* policy moves your VM to the stopped-deallocated state, allowing you to redeploy it later. However, there's no guarantee that the allocation will succeed. The deallocated VMs will count against your quota and you'll be charged storage costs for the underlying disks.

notes.front: A nightly image-processing job can restart from checkpoints if interrupted, and the budget is tight. Which option cuts compute cost most?
notes.back: Azure Spot Virtual Machines.
notes.choices:
A) Azure Spot Virtual Machines
B) Azure Dedicated Host
C) A proximity placement group
notes.choicesExplained: B: a dedicated host reserves a whole physical server, which costs more, not less. C: a proximity placement group reduces latency; it doesn't lower price.
notes.explanation: Spot machines use spare capacity at a large discount and suit workloads that can handle interruptions, such as batch jobs.
notes.source: Azure Spot Virtual Machines (MicrosoftDocs azure-compute-docs), “Azure Spot Virtual Machines”
notes.evidence: Therefore, Azure Spot Virtual Machines are great for workloads that can handle interruptions like batch processing jobs, dev/test environments, large compute workloads, and more.

notes.front: A payments service must run without interruption and needs an availability guarantee. Why are Spot virtual machines the wrong choice?
notes.back: They can be evicted at any time with 30 seconds' notice and have no service-level agreement.
notes.choices:
A) They can't run in a virtual network
B) They can be evicted at any time and have no service-level agreement
C) They only run Linux
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: neither restriction is stated for Spot; the documented drawback is eviction without an availability guarantee.
notes.explanation: Spot offers no high availability guarantees, so it suits only interruptible work.
notes.source: Azure Spot Virtual Machines (MicrosoftDocs azure-compute-docs), “Azure Spot Virtual Machines”
notes.evidence: An Azure Spot Virtual Machine offers no high availability guarantees.

notes.front: On an Azure Dedicated Host, can other customers' virtual machines run on your physical server?
notes.back: No; hardware isolation keeps other customers' machines off your hosts.
notes.explanation: Sensitive memory data stays isolated within a physical host, although network and storage infrastructure are still shared.
notes.source: Azure Dedicated Hosts (MicrosoftDocs azure-compute-docs), “Benefits”
notes.evidence: Security: Hardware isolation at the physical server level allows for sensitive memory data to remain isolated within a physical host. No other customer's VMs will be placed on your hosts. Dedicated hosts are deployed in the same data centers and share the same network and underlying storage infrastructure as other, non-isolated hosts.

notes.front: What control over Azure maintenance does a dedicated host give you?
notes.back: Near-complete control over platform-initiated maintenance, with an opt-in maintenance window.
notes.explanation: Some sensitive workloads are affected by each second of pause.
notes.source: Azure Dedicated Hosts (MicrosoftDocs azure-compute-docs), “Benefits”
notes.evidence: Reliability: You have near complete control over maintenance events initiated by the Azure platform. While most maintenance events have little to no impact on your virtual machines, there are some sensitive workloads where each second of pause can have an impact. With dedicated hosts, you can opt in to a maintenance window to reduce the impact to your service.

notes.front: A regulator requires that a bank's virtual machines never share physical hardware with other customers. Which option meets this?
notes.back: Azure Dedicated Host.
notes.choices:
A) Azure Dedicated Host
B) A proximity placement group
C) Azure Spot Virtual Machines
notes.choicesExplained: B: a proximity placement group keeps your machines close together, not away from other customers. C: Spot machines run on shared spare capacity.
notes.explanation: It isolates hardware at the physical server level, and no other customer's machines are placed on your hosts.
notes.source: Azure Dedicated Hosts (MicrosoftDocs azure-compute-docs), “Benefits”
notes.evidence: No other customer's VMs will be placed on your hosts.

notes.front: Why might machines in one availability zone still see latency between them, and what brings them closest?
notes.back: A zone may span several data centres; a proximity placement group puts machines as close as possible.
notes.explanation: Choosing a region or zone narrows the distance, but the docs say to deploy in a proximity placement group to get the lowest possible latency.
notes.source: Proximity placement groups (MicrosoftDocs azure-compute-docs), “Proximity placement groups”
notes.evidence: However, as the Azure footprint grows, a single availability zone may span multiple physical data centers, which may result in a network latency impacting your application. To get VMs as close as possible, achieving the lowest possible latency, you should deploy them within a proximity placement group.

notes.front: A trading platform's application tier and database tier must talk with the lowest possible network latency. What should you deploy them in?
notes.back: A proximity placement group.
notes.choices:
A) A proximity placement group
B) Azure Dedicated Host
C) Azure VMware Solution
notes.choicesExplained: B: a dedicated host isolates hardware from other customers; it isn't described as a latency tool. C: AVS runs VMware private clouds.
notes.explanation: It keeps compute resources physically close, and can bring together tiers of a multi-tier application.
notes.source: Proximity placement groups (MicrosoftDocs azure-compute-docs), “Proximity placement groups”
notes.evidence: Low latency between stand-alone VMs, VMs in multiple Availability Sets, or multiple scale sets. You can have multiple compute resources in a single placement group to bring together a multi-tiered application.

notes.front: Which managed disk type suits input/output-intensive workloads such as top-tier databases and other transaction-heavy work?
notes.back: Ultra Disk.
notes.explanation: Its scenario column names input/output-intensive, transaction-heavy work.
notes.source: Azure managed disk types (MicrosoftDocs azure-compute-docs), “Compare Azure managed disk types”
notes.evidence: I/O-intensive workloads such as SAP HANA, top-tier databases (for example, SQL Server and Oracle Database), and other transaction-heavy workloads.

notes.front: Which managed disk type generally costs less than Premium SSD yet performs better, with capacity and performance adjustable at any time?
notes.back: Premium SSD v2.
notes.explanation: Performance can be tuned as needs shift, which keeps workloads cost-efficient.
notes.source: Azure managed disk types (MicrosoftDocs azure-compute-docs), “Premium SSD v2”
notes.evidence: Premium SSD v2 offers higher performance than Premium SSDs while also generally being less costly. You can individually tweak the performance (capacity, throughput, and IOPS) of Premium SSD v2 disks at any time

notes.front: Which managed disk type is for production workloads needing high performance and low latency, and can also be an operating system disk?
notes.back: Premium SSD.
notes.explanation: Ultra Disk and Premium SSD v2 can't be used as operating system disks; Premium SSD can.
notes.source: Azure managed disk types (MicrosoftDocs azure-compute-docs), “Compare Azure managed disk types”
notes.evidence: Usable as OS Disk? | No | No | Yes | Yes |

notes.front: Which managed disk type is aimed at web servers, lightly used enterprise applications and development or test environments?
notes.back: Standard SSD.
notes.explanation: The scenario column lists these lighter workloads for it.
notes.source: Azure managed disk types (MicrosoftDocs azure-compute-docs), “Compare Azure managed disk types”
notes.evidence: Web servers, lightly used enterprise applications, and development and test environments.

notes.front: Which managed disk type is meant for backup and other noncritical, infrequently accessed workloads?
notes.back: Standard HDD.
notes.explanation: Its scenario column lists only noncritical, infrequently accessed work.
notes.source: Azure managed disk types (MicrosoftDocs azure-compute-docs), “Compare Azure managed disk types”
notes.evidence: Backup and other noncritical, infrequently accessed workloads.

notes.front: A top-tier transaction-heavy database needs the highest disk performance, with throughput changes made without restarting the machine. Which disk fits?
notes.back: Ultra Disks, as data disks.
notes.choices:
A) Ultra Disks
B) Standard SSD
C) Standard HDD
notes.choicesExplained: B: Standard SSD targets web servers and dev/test. C: Standard HDD targets backup and infrequently accessed data.
notes.explanation: Ultra Disks are the highest-performing option, and their performance can change without restarting the machine.
notes.source: Azure managed disk types (MicrosoftDocs azure-compute-docs), “Ultra Disks”
notes.evidence: Azure Ultra Disks are the highest-performing storage option for Azure virtual machines (VMs). You can change the performance parameters of an Ultra Disk without having to restart your VMs.

notes.front: A company runs hundreds of workloads on VMware vSphere and wants them in Azure while keeping vCenter and its VMware tools. Which service fits?
notes.back: Azure VMware Solution.
notes.choices:
A) Azure VMware Solution
B) Azure App Service
C) Azure Container Instances
notes.choicesExplained: B: App Service hosts web apps, not VMware virtual machines. C: ACI runs containers, not vSphere workloads.
notes.explanation: Its private clouds include vCenter Server, vSAN and vSphere, so workloads can migrate from on-premises.
notes.source: What is Azure VMware Solution? (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “What is Azure VMware Solution?”
notes.evidence: All provisioned private clouds have VMware vCenter Server, VMware vSAN, VMware vSphere, and VMware NSX. As a result, you can migrate workloads from your on-premises environments, deploy new virtual machines (VMs), and consume Azure services from your private clouds.

notes.front: What does each App Service plan define?
notes.back: Among others: operating system, region, number and size of machine instances, and pricing tier.
notes.explanation: These settings fix the compute that every app in the plan runs on.
notes.source: What are Azure App Service plans? (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “What are Azure App Service plans?”
notes.evidence: Each App Service plan defines: - Operating system (Windows, Linux) - Region (West US, East US, and so on) - Number of virtual machine (VM) instances - Size of VM instances (small, medium, large)

notes.front: Which App Service pricing tiers run your app on the same machine as other customers' apps?
notes.back: Free and Shared (the shared compute tiers).
notes.explanation: Each app gets a processor-time quota on the shared machine.
notes.source: What are Azure App Service plans? (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Pricing tiers”
notes.evidence: Free and Shared, the two base tiers, run an app on the same Azure VM as other App Service apps, including apps of other customers. These tiers allocate CPU quotas to each app that you run.

notes.front: Which App Service pricing tiers run apps on dedicated machines shared only by apps in the same plan?
notes.back: The dedicated compute tiers: Basic, Standard and the Premium tiers.
notes.explanation: Machines are dedicated to the plan, and only apps in that plan share them.
notes.source: What are Azure App Service plans? (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Pricing tiers”
notes.evidence: The Basic, Standard, Premium, PremiumV2, PremiumV3, and PremiumV4 tiers run apps on dedicated Azure VMs. Only apps in the same App Service plan share the same VM instances.

notes.front: Which App Service pricing tier adds network isolation on top of compute isolation?
notes.back: IsolatedV2.
notes.explanation: It runs dedicated machines on dedicated Azure virtual networks.
notes.source: What are Azure App Service plans? (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Pricing tiers”
notes.evidence: The IsolatedV2 tier runs dedicated Azure VMs on dedicated Azure virtual networks. This tier provides network isolation on top of compute isolation to your apps.

notes.front: What happens to the other apps in an App Service plan when you scale the plan out?
notes.back: They all scale together, because every app in the plan shares the same machine instances.
notes.explanation: Scaling the plan, manually or by autoscale, affects every app in it.
notes.source: What are Azure App Service plans? (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Considerations for running and scaling an app”
notes.evidence: All apps in an App Service plan scale together, because they share the same underlying compute resources (VM instances). Scaling the plan — whether manually or through autoscale rules — affects all apps in the plan.

notes.front: A busy public website and a rarely used admin app sit in one App Service plan, and the admin app slows when the site is busy. How do you isolate their compute?
notes.back: Move the admin app to a separate App Service plan.
notes.choices:
A) Scale the shared plan up to a larger size
B) Move the admin app to a separate App Service plan
C) Add a deployment slot to the admin app
notes.choicesExplained: A: a larger plan still shares its compute between both apps. C: deployment slots run on the same machine instances as the app.
notes.explanation: Only a separate plan gives the admin app compute of its own.
notes.source: What are Azure App Service plans? (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Cost of App Service plans”
notes.evidence: To isolate compute per app, create a separate App Service plan.

notes.front: A government web app must run on dedicated machines in a dedicated virtual network, isolated from other customers. Which App Service tier fits?
notes.back: IsolatedV2.
notes.choices:
A) Shared
B) Standard
C) IsolatedV2
notes.choicesExplained: A: Shared runs apps on machines shared with other customers. B: Standard gives dedicated machines but not dedicated virtual networks.
notes.explanation: It runs dedicated machines on dedicated virtual networks, adding network isolation to compute isolation.
notes.source: What are Azure App Service plans? (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Pricing tiers”
notes.evidence: The IsolatedV2 tier runs dedicated Azure VMs on dedicated Azure virtual networks. This tier provides network isolation on top of compute isolation to your apps. It provides a level of isolation from other customers.

notes.front: How quickly can Azure Container Instances start containers?
notes.back: In seconds, without provisioning or managing virtual machines.
notes.explanation: Containers offer significant startup benefits over virtual machines.
notes.source: What is Azure Container Instances? (MicrosoftDocs azure-compute-docs), “Fast startup times”
notes.evidence: Containers offer significant startup benefits over virtual machines (VMs). Azure Container Instances can start containers in Azure in seconds, without the need to provision and manage VMs.

notes.front: Does Azure Container Instances provide full container orchestration?
notes.back: No; it runs a single container or group without provisioning machines or adopting a higher-level service.
notes.explanation: It suits running a single container or a group of containers.
notes.source: Choose an Azure compute service (MicrosoftDocs architecture-center), “Understand the basic features”
notes.evidence: Azure Container Instances is a service for running a single container or group of containers in Azure. Container Instances doesn't provide full container orchestration, but you can implement containers without the need to provision VMs or adopt a higher-level service.

notes.front: A team needs to run a small container once an hour for a few minutes to tidy files, with no cluster to manage and no orchestration. Which service fits?
notes.back: Azure Container Instances.
notes.choices:
A) Azure Container Instances
B) Azure Kubernetes Service
C) Azure Virtual Machines
notes.choicesExplained: B: AKS brings a Kubernetes cluster and its operational overhead. C: virtual machines must be provisioned and managed.
notes.explanation: ACI runs containers without managing machines or adopting a higher-level service.
notes.source: What is Azure Container Instances? (MicrosoftDocs azure-compute-docs), “What is Azure Container Instances?”
notes.evidence: Azure Container Instances offers the fastest and simplest way to run Linux or Windows containers in Azure, without having to manage any virtual machines and without having to adopt a higher-level service.

notes.front: In AKS, who creates and manages the Kubernetes control plane, and what does it cost?
notes.back: Azure creates, configures and manages the control plane, at no cost to you.
notes.explanation: The control plane is responsible for the Kubernetes objects and worker nodes you deploy.
notes.source: What is Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)? (MicrosoftDocs azure-aks-docs), “Overview of AKS”
notes.evidence: When you create an AKS cluster, Azure automatically creates and configures a control plane for you at no cost. The Azure platform manages the AKS control plane, which is responsible for the Kubernetes objects and worker nodes that you deploy to run your applications.

notes.front: AKS Automatic versus AKS Standard: which mode suits platform teams that need full infrastructure control?
notes.back: AKS Standard; AKS Automatic suits developer teams, new workloads and production apps.
notes.explanation: The choice turns on how much infrastructure control the team needs.
notes.source: What is Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)? (MicrosoftDocs azure-aks-docs), “Choose your AKS mode”
notes.evidence: Best for | Developer teams, new workloads, quick onboarding, and production applications | Platform teams that require full infrastructure control

notes.front: A platform team needs Windows node pools and custom networking, and already has automation built around manual cluster management. Which AKS mode fits?
notes.back: AKS Standard.
notes.choices:
A) AKS Automatic
B) AKS Standard
C) Azure Container Apps
notes.choicesExplained: A: Automatic manages the infrastructure for you and is not the suggested mode for these needs. C: Container Apps doesn't give access to the Kubernetes control plane.
notes.explanation: Microsoft suggests Standard for custom networking, Windows node pools or existing manual-management automation.
notes.source: What is Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)? (MicrosoftDocs azure-aks-docs), “Choose your AKS mode”
notes.evidence: Use AKS Standard when you need custom networking configurations, Windows node pools, specific VM SKUs not yet available in Automatic, or have existing automation built around manual cluster management.

notes.front: AKS versus Azure Container Apps: which gives direct access to the Kubernetes APIs and control plane?
notes.back: AKS; Container Apps is built on Kubernetes but doesn't expose its APIs.
notes.explanation: The guide says to use AKS when you need the Kubernetes APIs and control plane.
notes.source: Choose an Azure compute service (MicrosoftDocs architecture-center), “Understand the basic features”
notes.evidence: It doesn't provide direct access to the underlying Kubernetes APIs. Use AKS if you require access to the Kubernetes APIs and control plane.

notes.front: Which Azure Container Apps applications can't scale to zero?
notes.back: Those that scale on processor or memory load.
notes.explanation: The documentation notes this as the exception to scaling to zero.
notes.source: Azure Container Apps overview (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Features”
notes.evidence: Applications that scale on CPU or memory load can't scale to zero.

notes.front: A team wants to run event-driven microservices in containers that scale to zero when idle, without learning Kubernetes. Which service fits?
notes.back: Azure Container Apps.
notes.choices:
A) Azure Container Apps
B) Azure Kubernetes Service
C) Azure Container Instances
notes.choicesExplained: B: AKS needs Kubernetes administration skills. C: ACI has no autoscaling or orchestration for microservices.
notes.explanation: The guide pairs Container Apps with teams that want modern patterns without Kubernetes complexity.
notes.source: Choose an Azure compute service (MicrosoftDocs architecture-center), “Team skills and operational overhead”
notes.evidence: | Container Apps | Container basics, cloud-native patterns | Low: Abstracted Kubernetes management | Teams that want modern patterns without Kubernetes complexity |

notes.front: How do Azure Functions connect to other services without extra code?
notes.back: Through event-driven triggers and bindings.
notes.explanation: They are the basis of the event-driven scenarios Functions supports.
notes.source: What is Azure Functions? (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Scenarios”
notes.evidence: Functions provides a comprehensive set of event-driven triggers and bindings that connect your functions to other services without having to write extra code.

notes.front: Up to how many instances can a function app scale out on the Flex Consumption plan?
notes.back: Up to 1,000.
notes.explanation: Instances scale on per-instance concurrency, incoming events and per-function workloads.
notes.source: Azure Functions hosting options (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Overview of plans”
notes.evidence: In the Flex Consumption plan, function instances dynamically scale out (up to 1,000) based on configured per-instance concurrency, incoming events, and per-function workloads for optimal efficiency.

notes.front: Which Functions hosting plan uses always-warm instances for the fastest response, unlimited execution duration and virtual network integration?
notes.back: The Premium plan.
notes.explanation: Always-warm instances give the fastest response times.
notes.source: What is Azure Functions? (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Hosting options”
notes.evidence: | Premium plan | Always-warm instances for the fastest response times, unlimited execution duration, and virtual network integration. |

notes.front: Which Functions hosting plan runs functions in an existing App Service plan with predictable scaling and costs?
notes.back: The Dedicated plan.
notes.explanation: It reuses an App Service plan you already run.
notes.source: What is Azure Functions? (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Hosting options”
notes.evidence: | Dedicated plan | Run functions in an existing App Service plan with predictable scaling and costs. |

notes.front: Which Functions hosting option deploys fully customised containerised function apps alongside microservices?
notes.back: Azure Container Apps.
notes.explanation: Function apps then run next to other microservices in the same environment.
notes.source: What is Azure Functions? (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Hosting options”
notes.evidence: | Container Apps | Deploy fully customized containerized function apps alongside microservices in Azure Container Apps. |

notes.front: What is the status of the Azure Functions Consumption plan?
notes.back: Legacy and Windows only (retired on Linux); new apps should use the Flex Consumption plan.
notes.explanation: Microsoft points all new serverless function apps to the Flex Consumption plan.
notes.source: What is Azure Functions? (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Hosting options”
notes.evidence: | Consumption plan | Legacy serverless plan (Windows only). Use the Flex Consumption plan for new apps. |

notes.front: A new serverless function app on Linux has spiky, event-driven load, must reach resources in a virtual network, and should cost nothing when idle. Which plan fits?
notes.back: The Flex Consumption plan.
notes.choices:
A) The Consumption plan on Linux
B) The Flex Consumption plan
C) A Dedicated (App Service) plan
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Consumption plan is legacy and retired on Linux. C: a Dedicated plan runs on App Service instances that you pay for even when idle.
notes.explanation: It gives serverless pay-as-you-go billing, virtual network connectivity and rapid event-driven scaling.
notes.source: Azure Functions hosting options (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Overview of plans”
notes.evidence:
You need a serverless host for your function code, paying only for on-demand executions.
✔ You require virtual network connectivity for secure access to Azure resources.
✔ Your workloads are variable and can go from no activity to demanding rapid, event-driven scaling.

notes.front: Function apps run almost continuously, must respond with no cold-start delay, and need more memory than serverless plans give. Which plan fits?
notes.back: The Premium plan.
notes.choices:
A) The Premium plan
B) The Consumption plan
C) The Flex Consumption plan with no always-ready instances
notes.choicesExplained: B: the Consumption plan scales to zero, so requests can meet startup delays. C: without always-ready instances Flex can also scale to zero when idle.
notes.explanation: It suits continuously running apps and uses prewarmed workers that run with no delay after being idle.
notes.source: Azure Functions hosting options (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Overview of plans”
notes.evidence: Automatically scales based on demand using prewarmed workers, which run applications with no delay after being idle, runs on more powerful instances, and connects to virtual networks.

notes.front: What are the default and maximum function timeouts on the legacy Consumption plan?
notes.back: 5 minutes by default and 10 minutes at most.
notes.explanation: These limits apply to function executions on that plan.
notes.source: Azure Functions hosting options (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Function app timeout duration”
notes.evidence: | Consumption plan | 5 | 10 |

notes.front: How many prebuilt connectors does Azure Logic Apps offer for integrating systems?
notes.back: More than 1,400.
notes.explanation: They cover Azure services, Microsoft services, external apps, databases and on-premises systems.
notes.source: What is Azure Logic Apps? (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Why use Azure Logic Apps?”
notes.evidence: Integrate systems faster: Choose from 1,400+ prebuilt Microsoft-managed connectors for Azure services, Microsoft services, external apps, databases, and on-premises systems.

notes.front: Consumption versus Standard logic app: which supports multiple workflows in single-tenant Azure Logic Apps?
notes.back: Standard; a Consumption logic app supports a single workflow in multitenant Azure Logic Apps.
notes.explanation: The resource type decides how many workflows it holds and where they run.
notes.source: What is Azure Logic Apps? (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Key terms”
notes.evidence:
A Consumption logic app resource that supports a single workflow, which is hosted and run in multitenant Azure Logic Apps

- A Standard logic app resource that supports multiple workflows, which are hosted and run in single-tenant Azure Logic Apps

notes.front: Which kind of logic app can reach secured resources in an Azure virtual network?
notes.back: A Standard logic app.
notes.explanation: Standard is a single-tenant instance with dedicated resources, running apart from multitenant Logic Apps.
notes.source: What is Azure Logic Apps? (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Azure Logic Apps capabilities”
notes.evidence: When you use Azure Logic Apps (Standard), your workflows can access secured resources such as virtual machines, other services, and systems in an Azure virtual network. Azure Logic Apps (Standard) is a single-tenant instance of Azure Logic Apps that uses dedicated resources and runs separately from global, multitenant Azure Logic Apps.

notes.front: Several related integration workflows must reach secured systems inside an Azure virtual network and run on dedicated resources. Which logic app type fits?
notes.back: A Standard logic app.
notes.choices:
A) A Consumption logic app
B) A Standard logic app
C) One Consumption logic app per workflow
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: Consumption logic apps run in shared multitenant Logic Apps, each with a single workflow, not on dedicated resources.
notes.explanation: Standard hosts multiple workflows single-tenant with dedicated resources and can reach resources in a virtual network.
notes.source: What is Azure Logic Apps? (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Azure Logic Apps capabilities”
notes.evidence: When you use Azure Logic Apps (Standard), your workflows can access secured resources such as virtual machines, other services, and systems in an Azure virtual network.

notes.front: Azure Logic Apps versus Azure Functions for orchestration: which is designer-first and which is code-first?
notes.back: Logic Apps is designer-first; Functions is code-first, using the Durable Functions extension.
notes.explanation: Each can call the other, so the choice rests on how the team prefers to build.
notes.source: What is Azure Logic Apps? (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Choose the appropriate automation service”
notes.evidence: | Azure Logic Apps | Designer-first automated orchestration workflows for enterprise business processes across services, systems, applications, and data sources. Can call functions in Azure Functions. | | Azure Functions | Code-first automated orchestrations using the Durable Functions extension. Can call workflows in Azure Logic Apps. |

notes.front: Business analysts want to build an approval process that routes orders over a set value to a manager and emails the result, using a visual designer and prebuilt connectors. What fits?
notes.back: Azure Logic Apps.
notes.choices:
A) Azure Logic Apps
B) Azure Functions with Durable Functions
C) Azure Batch
notes.choicesExplained: B: Durable Functions orchestrations are code-first. C: Batch runs large parallel compute jobs, not business workflows.
notes.explanation: Logic Apps offers designer-first workflows with prebuilt connectors and little or no code.
notes.source: What is Azure Logic Apps? (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Choose the appropriate automation service”
notes.evidence: Designer-first automated orchestration workflows for enterprise business processes across services, systems, applications, and data sources.

notes.front: What does it cost to use Azure Batch itself?
notes.back: Nothing extra; you pay only for the underlying resources, such as virtual machines, storage and networking.
notes.explanation: The charges come from the virtual machines, storage and networking it uses.
notes.source: What is Azure Batch? (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “What is Azure Batch?”
notes.evidence: There's no extra charge to use Batch. You pay only for the underlying resources consumed, such as virtual machines, storage, and networking.

notes.front: What kind of workload does Azure Batch handle particularly well?
notes.back: Intrinsically parallel workloads, where application instances run independently, each completing part of the work.
notes.explanation: Each instance completes its own part of the work independently.
notes.source: What is Azure Batch? (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Run parallel workloads”
notes.evidence: Batch works well with intrinsically parallel (also known as "embarrassingly parallel") workloads. These workloads have applications which can run independently, with each instance completing part of the work.

notes.front: In a Batch workflow, what do you create after uploading input files and applications to storage?
notes.back: A pool of compute nodes, a job to run the workload on the pool, and tasks in the job.
notes.explanation: The job runs the workload on the pool, and its tasks make up the work.
notes.source: What is Azure Batch? (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “How it works”
notes.evidence: Create a Batch pool of compute nodes in your Batch account, a job to run the workload on the pool, and tasks in the job.

notes.front: If existing scheduler-specific job scripts and queues must stay in place, what does Microsoft suggest instead of Batch?
notes.back: Azure CycleCloud, which preserves the scheduler operating model.
notes.explanation: Moving those workflows to Batch would mean translating them into Batch pools, jobs and tasks.
notes.source: What is Azure Batch? (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Choose an Azure service for batch and HPC workloads”
notes.evidence: Moving those workflows to Batch would require translating them into Batch pools, jobs, and tasks. CycleCloud preserves the scheduler operating model.

notes.front: A bank must run 50,000 independent Monte Carlo risk simulations overnight on hundreds of machines, without installing or running scheduler software. What fits?
notes.back: Azure Batch.
notes.choices:
A) Azure Batch
B) Azure Logic Apps
C) Azure Container Instances
notes.choicesExplained: B: Logic Apps automates business workflows, not large parallel compute. C: ACI runs individual containers without job scheduling across a pool of nodes.
notes.explanation: Monte Carlo financial risk modelling is one of Microsoft's examples of an intrinsically parallel Batch workload.
notes.source: What is Azure Batch? (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Run parallel workloads”
notes.evidence: Some examples of intrinsically parallel workloads you can bring to Batch: - Financial risk modeling using Monte Carlo simulations
